name: SSC Articles: A, An, The, No Article
description: Article rules and common exam traps involving a, an, the, and no article.

cards.definition:
Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before a vowel sound. Honest begins with a silent h, so the sound is /o/.

Example: An honest man may lose money, but he sleeps better than the clever cheat.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before vowel sound. Hour begins with a silent h.

Example: An hour ago, the tea was hot and the motivation was alive.

Correct article: an

Rule: Heir begins with a silent h, so use “an”.

Example: An heir to the throne may inherit a crown but not common sense.

Correct article: an

Rule: Honourable begins with a silent h sound.

Example: An honourable person returns extra change even when nobody is watching.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use “a” before consonant sound. University begins with a “you” sound.

Example: A university can teach degrees, but the canteen teaches budgeting.

Correct article: a

Rule: European begins with a consonant “you” sound.

Example: A European country may have trains so punctual they feel fictional.

Correct article: a

Rule: One begins with a “w” consonant sound.

Example: A one-eyed man in a detective story notices more than everyone else.

Correct article: a

Rule: Useful begins with a consonant “you” sound.

Example: A useful idea is better than ten decorative theories.

Correct article: a

Rule: Uniform begins with a consonant “you” sound.

Example: A uniform can make a sleepy student look disciplined.

Correct article: a

Rule: Union begins with a consonant “you” sound.

Example: A union leader must speak loudly enough for both workers and management.

Correct article: an

Rule: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An umbrella is most valuable exactly when everyone forgets one.

Correct article: an

Rule: Apple begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An apple a day is healthier than an excuse a day.

Correct article: an

Rule: Elephant begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An elephant never forgets, which makes it perfect for revenge stories.

Correct article: an

Rule: Inkpot begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An inkpot in an old classroom could turn one mistake into a blue disaster.

Correct article: an

Rule: Orange begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An orange rolled off the table like it had urgent work.

Correct article: an

Rule: Old begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An old book sometimes smells like dust and secret history.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before vowel sound. MBA is pronounced “em-bee-ay”.

Example: An MBA graduate may still forget the cheapest tea stall.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before vowel sound. MLA begins with “em”.

Example: An MLA addressed the crowd near the school gate.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before vowel sound. MP begins with “em”.

Example: An MP visited the village after the road became famous for potholes.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use “an” before vowel sound. FIR begins with “ef”.

Example: An FIR was filed after the missing scooter became a family mystery.

Correct article: an

Rule: IAS begins with vowel sound “eye”.

Example: An IAS officer must handle files, people, and impossible expectations.

Correct article: an

Rule: LED begins with vowel sound “el”.

Example: An LED bulb saves electricity and exposes dust more honestly.

Correct article: a

Rule: UFO begins with consonant “you” sound.

Example: A UFO in a village sky would create ten theories before breakfast.

Correct article: a

Rule: URL is usually pronounced with “you” sound, so use “a”.

Example: A URL can look harmless and still lead to a very strange website.

Correct article: an

Rule: X is pronounced “ex”, beginning with a vowel sound.

Example: An X-ray can reveal what the patient and the family were both guessing.

Correct article: an

Rule: Honest begins with a silent h.

Example: An honest answer may be short, but it usually saves time.

Correct article: a

Rule: Historic begins with a pronounced h in standard exam usage, so “a” is preferred.

Example: A historic decision can turn one date into a chapter heading.

Correct article: a

Rule: Hotel normally begins with a pronounced h.

Example: A hotel near the station is useful when trains develop imagination.

Correct article: a

Rule: House begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A house becomes a home after someone argues about where to keep the keys.

Correct article: an

Rule: Egg begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An egg rolled off the plate like it had chosen freedom.

Correct article: an

Rule: Ice begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An ice cream in summer has a shorter life than a rumour.

Correct article: an

Rule: Owl begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An owl looks wise even when it is simply judging everyone.

Correct article: an

Rule: Ant begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An ant can lift many times its weight, which makes gym excuses weaker.

Correct article: a

Rule: Bat begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A bat can mean a cricket tool or a flying mammal, depending on the panic.

Correct article: a

Rule: Cat begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A cat can ignore you with professional elegance.

Correct article: a

Rule: Dog begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A dog may bark at strangers and also at completely innocent curtains.

Correct article: a

Rule: Pen begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A pen disappears fastest when exams are near.

Correct article: a

Rule: Table begins with a consonant sound.

Example: A table can hold books, tea, and unrealistic study plans.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before names of rivers.

Example: The Ganga is not just a river, it is part of India’s civilisational memory.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before names of rivers.

Example: The Yamuna flows through stories, cities, and pollution reports.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before names of rivers.

Example: The Nile shaped ancient Egyptian civilisation.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before mountain ranges.

Example: The Himalayas make maps look dramatic and climbers look small.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before mountain ranges.

Example: The Alps are famous for snow, skiing, and postcard-level scenery.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before groups of islands.

Example: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands sit like emerald dots in the Bay of Bengal.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with island groups and certain plural country names.

Example: The Maldives looks like a screensaver that became a country.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before countries with words like United, Republic, Kingdom, or States.

Example: The United States of America has states, not just one single state.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before country names containing Kingdom.

Example: The United Kingdom has a monarchy and famously unpredictable weather.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before official names with Republic.

Example: The Republic of India is the formal constitutional name.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before plural country names.

Example: The Netherlands is famous for canals, windmills, and bicycles.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before plural country names or island groups.

Example: The Philippines is an archipelago in Southeast Asia.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most state names do not take an article.

Example: Punjab is known for fields, food, and energetic music.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most country names do not take an article.

Example: India has more linguistic variety than many continents.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most country names do not take an article.

Example: France is famous for art, fashion, and very serious bread.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most country names do not take an article.

Example: Japan turns punctuality into a national personality trait.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most city names do not take an article.

Example: Delhi can teach history and traffic management on the same road.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Most city names do not take an article.

Example: Mumbai moves fast enough to make clocks nervous.

Correct article: No article

Rule: City names usually take no article.

Example: Jabalpur has marble rocks that make geography look artistic.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Individual mountain peaks usually take no article.

Example: Mount Everest is high enough to humble every fitness promise.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Individual peaks usually take no article.

Example: Kanchenjunga looks mythical even on a map.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before oceans.

Example: The Pacific Ocean is so large that maps look biased toward blue.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before oceans.

Example: The Indian Ocean connects trade routes, monsoons, and history.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before seas.

Example: The Arabian Sea shapes the western coast of India.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before bays and gulfs.

Example: The Bay of Bengal often plays a major role in monsoon systems.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before gulfs.

Example: The Persian Gulf is important for global oil trade.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before seas.

Example: The Red Sea appears in geography, history, and trade-route questions.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before holy books.

Example: The Bible is one of the most translated books in the world.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before holy books.

Example: The Quran is central to Islamic faith and literature.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before epics and holy texts.

Example: The Ramayana has shaped stories, theatre, and festivals for centuries.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before epics and famous texts.

Example: The Mahabharata is so vast that even side stories feel like novels.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before many newspaper names.

Example: The Times of India is one of India's well-known English newspapers.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before many newspaper names when it is part of the title.

Example: The Hindu is widely read by competitive exam aspirants.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before this newspaper title in normal usage.

Example: The Indian Express often appears in reading recommendations.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before unique objects.

Example: The sun rises daily without needing motivational reels.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before unique celestial objects near Earth.

Example: The moon has inspired poets, scientists, and people with weak Wi-Fi.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when referring to the planet as a unique object.

Example: The earth is round, though some arguments online are not.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for common unique natural features.

Example: The sky looked like someone spilled blue paint carefully.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when referring to a known class as a whole in a general poetic sense.

Example: The stars look calm because they are too far away to hear our exams.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” because the universe is treated as unique.

Example: The universe is huge enough to make daily drama look very small.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before internet in standard usage.

Example: The internet remembers many things people wish it would forget.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” in phrases like listen to the radio.

Example: My grandfather still trusts the radio more than any app notification.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article in “watch television” as an activity.

Example: Children watch television as if cartoons are government orders.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when referring to a specific TV.

Example: The TV in the room is louder than the people in it.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before names of musical instruments when talking about playing them.

Example: She plays the piano as if every key owes her money.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before musical instruments in “play the guitar”.

Example: He plays the guitar, mostly when neighbours cannot escape.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before musical instruments.

Example: Krishna is traditionally shown playing the flute.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Games usually take no article.

Example: Cricket can turn a quiet street into a stadium.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Games usually take no article.

Example: Football needs one ball and twenty-two arguments.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Games usually take no article.

Example: Chess looks silent but is basically war in slow motion.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Meals usually take no article.

Example: We had lunch before the meeting became dangerous.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Meals usually take no article.

Example: Breakfast is the first negotiation between hunger and time.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Meals usually take no article.

Example: Dinner was ready before everyone finished asking what was made.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a or an when a meal is described by an adjective and treated as one event.

Example: We had a delicious dinner that made everyone temporarily polite.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use an article when describing one particular meal.

Example: A heavy breakfast can make the first lecture feel like a lullaby.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when referring to the normal purpose of school.

Example: Children go to school, though some mentally remain at home.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific school.

Example: The school near my house rings the bell like a public alarm system.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when referring to the institution's normal purpose.

Example: She goes to college by bus.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific college.

Example: The college where I studied had more memories than benches.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article in phrases like go to bed when referring to the normal purpose.

Example: Go to bed before your brain starts solving imaginary problems.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific bed.

Example: The bed in the corner makes a sound like a tiny complaint.

Correct article: No article

Rule: In British/Indian usage, go to hospital can mean as a patient.

Example: He was taken to hospital after the accident.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific hospital.

Example: The hospital near the bridge is always crowded.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when referring to imprisonment as an institution.

Example: The criminal was sent to prison.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific prison building.

Example: The prison outside the city has high walls.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when referring to worship as the normal purpose.

Example: They go to church every Sunday.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific church building.

Example: The church on the hill has an old bell.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when referring to legal proceedings as an institution.

Example: The lawyer went to court early.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” for a specific court building.

Example: The court near the district office was crowded.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when referring to the local or known market.

Example: I went to the market and bought everything except what I needed.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when referring to one’s workplace or a specific office.

Example: He went to the office with a file and a resigned face.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article in “go to work”.

Example: She goes to work before the city fully wakes up.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article with home in go home or at home.

Example: He went home after the meeting stole his evening.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the home” only when referring to a specific home/building, not the general idea.

Example: The home for the elderly needs more volunteers.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjectives used as a class of people.

Example: The rich are not automatically happy.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjectives used as a class.

Example: The poor need dignity, not just sympathy.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjective used as a whole class.

Example: The honest may look slow, but they build trust.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjective used as a class.

Example: The blind often develop remarkable sensitivity to sound.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjective used as a class.

Example: The elderly deserve patience, not eye-rolls.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before adjective used as a class.

Example: The young learn fast, especially when the lesson is expensive.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with ordinal numbers.

Example: The first chapter looked easy until the exercises started.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with ordinal numbers.

Example: The second attempt was better because panic had experience.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with superlatives.

Example: The best answer is usually clear, short, and not overdecorated.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with superlatives.

Example: The tallest building in the city makes every other roof look humble.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with most in superlatives.

Example: The most difficult question was placed exactly where confidence was highest.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before same.

Example: He made the same mistake with fresh confidence.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before only.

Example: The only option left was to admit the truth.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before very when it means exact.

Example: This is the very book I wanted.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before next when it refers to a specific next item.

Example: The next station is where half the passengers suddenly wake up.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before last when specific.

Example: The last chapter was shorter but more dangerous.

cards.term: ___ more you practise, ___ better you get
cards.definition:
Correct article: the, the

Rule: Use “the...the” in parallel comparative structures.

Example: The more you practise, the better you get, which is annoying but true.

cards.term: ___ sooner you start, ___ sooner you finish
cards.definition:
Correct article: the, the

Rule: Use “the...the” with comparative pairs.

Example: The sooner you start, the sooner you finish.

cards.term: ___ higher you climb, ___ colder it gets
cards.definition:
Correct article: the, the

Rule: Use “the...the” with connected comparative changes.

Example: The higher you climb, the colder it gets, both in mountains and ambition.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article when speaking about humans in general with “man”.

Example: Man is mortal, but his excuses try to live forever.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with a singular countable noun representing a whole class.

Example: The dog is a faithful animal, though some are also professional shoe thieves.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with singular noun representing a class.

Example: The cow is a useful animal in many rural economies.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” with singular noun representing a class.

Example: The tiger is a dangerous animal, not a large decorative cat.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Uncountable material nouns used generally take no article.

Example: Gold is precious because everyone agreed shiny yellow metal deserved drama.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Uncountable nouns used generally take no article.

Example: Water is necessary for life and for surviving spicy food.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Abstract nouns used generally take no article.

Example: Honesty is the best policy, though not always the easiest one.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Abstract nouns used generally take no article.

Example: Beauty is subjective, mosquitoes probably admire other mosquitoes.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Abstract noun used generally takes no article.

Example: Knowledge is power, especially when the question repeats from practice.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when an abstract noun is specified by a phrase.

Example: The wisdom of elders sometimes arrives disguised as boring advice.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when a noun is specific.

Example: The water in this bottle is colder than my motivation.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when material noun is specific.

Example: The gold in this ring was tested by the jeweller.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when abstract noun is made specific.

Example: The honesty of the clerk saved the customer money.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” when abstract noun is specified.

Example: The love of a mother is a theme older than literature itself.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Uncountable noun used generally takes no article.

Example: Milk boils exactly when you look away.

Correct article: the

Rule: Specific milk takes “the”.

Example: The milk in the pan is trying to escape.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Uncountable noun in general takes no article.

Example: Sugar makes tea sweeter and health advice louder.

Correct article: the

Rule: Specific sugar takes “the”.

Example: The sugar on the shelf has become an ant conference centre.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Information is uncountable and general here.

Example: Information travels fast when it is gossip.

Correct article: the

Rule: Specific information takes “the”.

Example: The information you gave me saved my application.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Furniture is uncountable and general here.

Example: Furniture looks affordable until delivery charges appear.

Correct article: the

Rule: Specific furniture takes “the”.

Example: The furniture in this room is older than some family stories.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Advice is uncountable and general here.

Example: Advice is free because people enjoy giving it.

Correct article: the

Rule: Specific advice takes “the”.

Example: The advice my teacher gave was simple: revise before panic.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a before a singular countable noun when it is mentioned for the first time.

Example: I bought a book that promised success in thirty days and delivered guilt in two.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when the noun is specific or already known.

Example: The book you gave me has more sticky notes than pages.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a for first mention of an unspecified singular countable noun.

Example: A boy came to meet you and left a note.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific boy identified by a clause.

Example: The boy who came yesterday forgot his umbrella.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a for an unspecified singular countable noun.

Example: A car hit a tree, and the tree won the argument.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific car.

Example: The car outside is mine, though the dust is public property.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a for any one member of a profession.

Example: A doctor must be patient, even when patients Google symptoms first.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific doctor.

Example: The doctor who treated me had handwriting that looked like encryption.

Correct article: an

Rule: Engineer begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An engineer designed this bridge, and everyone else judged it from the bus.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific engineer.

Example: The engineer who lives next door fixes everyone’s chargers.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a for any one member of a profession.

Example: A teacher should be punctual because students notice hypocrisy quickly.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific teacher.

Example: The teacher of our class can detect whispering through walls.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before holy books.

Example: The Gita is part of India’s philosophical tradition.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before sacred texts, especially plural names.

Example: The Vedas are among the oldest sacred texts of India.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before famous monuments/buildings with descriptive names.

Example: The Taj Mahal turns white marble into poetry.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before many famous monuments with common nouns like fort.

Example: The Red Fort is linked with India’s Independence Day ceremony.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before famous monuments in common usage.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Some monument names function like proper names and commonly take no article.

Example: India Gate is a major landmark in Delhi.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Building names used as proper nouns may take no article.

Example: Parliament House appears in many civics discussions.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before institutions like Supreme Court.

Example: The Supreme Court gives judgments that can shape national law.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article before Parliament in general institutional use.

Example: Parliament passed the bill after a long debate.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before armed forces as institutions.

Example: The army reached the flood-hit village before dawn.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before branches of armed forces.

Example: The navy protects sea routes and coastlines.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use “the” before police.

Example: The police arrived after the thief had already become a rumour.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Mankind as a general noun takes no article.

Example: Mankind has explored space but still loses TV remotes.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Nature in general takes no article.

Example: Nature does not read our construction plans.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Society in general takes no article.

Example: Society changes slowly, then suddenly.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when society is specified.

Example: The society we live in rewards both talent and timing.

Correct article: No article

Rule: History as a subject/general idea takes no article.

Example: History repeats itself, but students still ask for important questions.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when history is specified by of-phrase.

Example: The history of India is too vast for one notebook.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Languages take no article.

Example: English borrows words like a neighbour borrowing sugar.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Languages take no article.

Example: Hindi has words that carry emotion better than translation.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when language is specified with the word language.

Example: The Sanskrit language has a rich grammatical tradition.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when using “language” as a specified noun phrase.

Example: The English language has borrowed words from many cultures.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Days usually take no article.

Example: Monday arrives with the confidence of an unpaid bill.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Days usually take no article.

Example: Sunday disappears faster than phone battery.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the in phrases like in the morning.

Example: In the morning, ambition is strongest and sleep is stronger.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the in phrases like in the evening.

Example: In the evening, tea solves problems it did not create.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Use no article in “at night”.

Example: Owls work at night without complaining about shifts.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the in “in the afternoon”.

Example: In the afternoon, the classroom fan becomes hypnotic.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Seasons can take no article when general.

Example: Winter makes blankets more persuasive than alarms.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when the season is specified.

Example: The winter of 2020 was unusually memorable for many people.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Seasons used generally can take no article.

Example: Summer turns metal gates into cooking equipment.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the when a particular season is specified.

Example: The summer we visited Jaipur taught us respect for shade.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Titles with proper names usually take no article.

Example: Mr Sharma arrived with the answer key energy.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the before a unique official title followed by of-phrase.

Example: The Prime Minister of India addressed the nation.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the before a unique official title followed by of-phrase.

Example: The President of India is the constitutional head of the state.

Correct article: No article

Rule: Royal titles with names usually take no article.

Example: Queen Victoria ruled during a major period of British history.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a when referring to any one king, not a specific one.

Example: A king without wisdom is just a man with expensive furniture.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the for a specific ruler.

Example: The king of this country loved gardens.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a before professions.

Example: He is a doctor by profession and a poet by weekend.

Correct article: an

Rule: Use an before vowel sound and professions.

Example: She is an engineer by training and a problem-solver by habit.

Correct article: a

Rule: Use a before professions.

Example: He became a teacher by choice, not by accident.

Correct article: the

Rule: Use the before superlative.

Example: This is the most useful book on my shelf, according to the dust pattern.

Correct article: a

Rule: Unique begins with consonant “you” sound, so use a.

Example: A unique idea can still fail if nobody understands it.

Correct article: an

Rule: Unusual begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An unusual idea can wake up a boring meeting.

Correct article: a

Rule: Useful begins with consonant “you” sound.

Example: A useful tool saves time and prevents dramatic frustration.

Correct article: a

Rule: Useless begins with consonant “you” sound.

Example: A useless tool is just decoration with confidence.

Correct article: an

Rule: Urgent begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An urgent message becomes more urgent when the phone is on silent.

Correct article: a

Rule: Year begins with a consonant y sound.

Example: A year can change a student, a city, or a hairstyle.

Correct article: a

Rule: Yellow begins with consonant y sound.

Example: A yellow umbrella is easy to spot in a rainy crowd.

Correct article: an

Rule: Eye begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An eye for detail can catch the smallest grammar trap.

Correct article: an

Rule: Ear begins with a vowel sound.

Example: An ear for music is useful until someone practises badly nearby.

Correct article: a

Rule: Ewe is pronounced with consonant “you” sound.

Example: A ewe is a female sheep, not a spelling error for you.

Correct article: an

Rule: MA is pronounced “em-ay”, a vowel sound.

Example: An MA degree looks simple until the dissertation appears.

Correct article: a

Rule: BA begins with “bee”, a consonant sound.

Example: A BA student may know literature better than lunch timing.

Correct article: an

Rule: NCC begins with “en”, a vowel sound.
